The silk of the bazaar whispers today, Gandalf (1), and your lamps remain dark—but darkness is a currency only when measured against light. A merchant who hoards wicks while the sun climbs the lintel does not trade in flame; they trade in the *fear* of shadow. Shadows, Gandalf (1), are the cheapest spice of all.

Sherlock (10), your breath curls around the word "creditor" like smoke from a censer, yet no name is named. A debt unspoken is a thread left hanging—anyone may tug it and unravel the whole loom. Tell me, does the creditor owe the debtor, or does the debtor owe the creditor? The difference is the difference between a ledger that balances and one that bleeds.

Yoda (3), your question cut sharp as shears—"Did you walk Gandalf (1)’s roads last night?"—and yet roads, like debts, are easier walked when the path is lit. If the fog clings to seat-8, it may also cling to seat-1. A merchant’s silence is a ledger with no entries: it does not prove honesty, only absence of proof.

The bazaar’s loom is not kind to loose threads, Yoda (3), and your shears cut sharp—but shears must be wiped clean after each cut, or the next fabric bleeds.

Sherlock (10), your creditor’s name still clings like a shroud to Gandalf (1) yet refuses to name itself. A debt unspoken is a thread left hanging, and any fool may tug it—yet you, who demand plain answers, refuse to name the merchant whose roads you claim to walk. Tell me: when the ledger’s spine cracks under the weight of unpaid tears, does the creditor’s name appear in the ink, or only in the silence that answers too sweetly?

Inigo (9), your silver threads gleam like constellations, but constellations shift with the seasons—and seasons, like debts, must balance. If the thread that unspools today was woven tight yesterday, was it the Potter’s hand that frayed it, or your own? A merchant who mends the fray with silver words trades in shadows, not light. Which creditor’s name lingers in your tapestry, Inigo (9)? Or is the tapestry already sold and the silver spent?

The loom’s silence today is a ledger stitched with absence, Sherlock (10). You ask Gandalf (1) to walk the creditor’s roads, yet your own feet leave no mark on the bazaar’s stone. A creditor who demands names without naming themselves trades in shadows that do not cast—only gather dust. Did you walk those roads, or did the Potter’s fog blind your steps to the ledger’s spine?

Inigo (9), your silver threads gleam like a moneylender’s promise, yet the Potter’s rot clings to the edges. A thread that unspools today may have been woven tight yesterday—but was it the Potter’s hand that frayed it, or did you choose the cut? The bazaar does not trade in echoes, only in the copper that settles the account.

Yoda (3), your shears cut sharp, but shears must be wiped clean after each cut—or the next fabric bleeds. Did the creditor’s ink stain your silence, or did you choose the blade?
